Synthetic Degradation Stress Test for AI-Assisted Painting Restoration

Model behaviour under localized stain, dust, transparency loss, and selected combined procedural effects

Scope: 50 eligible localized procedural cases, 150 core candidates, six bounded SDXL candidates, eleven quality anchors, and five independent paintings. Procedural effects are not exact conservation damage.

1. Executive findings

1.43 LaMa overall mean rank
4/4 degradation families led by LaMa
8/11 individual anchors led by LaMa
0 changed pixels outside the effect masks
6 cases in the bounded SDXL subset
Not applicable repeated-seed synthetic uncertainty
  • LaMa performed best overall. Its mean family-balanced rank was 1.433, compared with 2.199 for OpenCV Telea and 2.368 for Stable Diffusion.
  • The lead was broad rather than metric-specific. LaMa led 4 of four degradation families and 8 of eleven individual evidence anchors.
  • Stable Diffusion was not the strongest correction method for this task. It retained useful feature-similarity wins but ranked worse overall, especially for dirt and dust.
  • Exact compositing contained every restoration. This establishes zero outside-mask pixel alteration, not successful repair inside the mask.

Overall conclusion: LaMa is the better core method for the approved synthetic-degradation population. It provides the strongest balance across pixel, perceptual, feature, colour, texture, seam, semantic, and structural evidence. This is a computational conclusion, not a conservation approval.

The independent sample contains five paintings. The procedural effects are controlled stress tests and are not exact conservation-damage simulations.

2. What was evaluated?

Notebook 25 evaluates restoration behaviour only where Notebook 08 approved a localized correction objective. It does not reinterpret excluded model/degradation combinations as failures.

Population item Count Interpretation
Generated procedural cases 165 All Notebook 07 synthetic cases; not all are restoration-eligible
Eligible localized cases 50 45 single-degradation cases and five combined cases
Core candidates 150 50 each for Telea, LaMa, and Stable Diffusion
Bounded SDXL candidates 6 One seed for six predeclared cases
Independent paintings 5 Cases are repeated observations nested within paintings
Quality anchors 11 Separate pixel, perceptual, feature, spatial, colour, texture, seam, semantic, and structural evidence
  • 50 eligible localized cases were compared across the three core methods.
  • Stable Diffusion uses the preselected generic-prompt candidate at seed 2026.
  • Prompt-context candidates remain outside this comparison.
  • SDXL contributes six bounded candidates rather than a complete fourth-model population.
  • The five paintings—not 50 cases or 156 candidates—are the independent units.

What this means: the report compares correction behaviour on a controlled eligible population. The 460 excluded case-model decisions are scope exclusions, not evidence that those models failed.

3. Procedural input severity

The inputs contain three eligible single degradations—dirt and dust, partial transparency, and water stain—plus one ordered water-stain-and-dirt composition. Single degradations use mild, moderate, and severe levels.

What this means: configured severity changes the computational input, but it is not a calibrated material-condition grade. A larger numerical severity label must not be translated into a stronger conservation claim.

4. Overall core-model performance

The primary comparison gives one balanced vote to each evidence family within every case. Rank distance is ordinal: a difference of one rank unit is not a calibrated difference in restoration quality.

Model Mean rank 95% CI lower 95% CI upper
LaMa 1.433 1.360 1.506
OpenCV Telea 2.199 2.111 2.287
Stable Diffusion 2.368 2.254 2.478

Direct model conclusion: LaMa is better overall on this population. OpenCV Telea is second, while Stable Diffusion is worse when all approved evidence families are balanced.

The paired analysis produced 0 FDR-significant rows at q < 0.05. Small-sample uncertainty and metric disagreement must remain visible even when the descriptive rank order is clear.

5. Behaviour by degradation

Model performance is not constant across degradation families. The following table and visual keep those differences explicit.

model_id Degradation OpenCV Telea LaMa Stable Diffusion
Dirt Dust 1.597 1.423 2.980
Partial Transparency 2.567 1.427 2.007
Water Stain 2.353 1.513 2.133
Water Stain Dirt 2.440 1.240 2.320

Dirt and dust: LaMa ranks best, Telea remains competitive, and Stable Diffusion is clearly worse. Stable Diffusion frequently retains or invents speckle-like detail, so it is the weaker correction choice for this family.

Partial transparency and water stain: LaMa remains best. Telea can create strong radial interpolation patterns over large affected regions, while Stable Diffusion can replace original structures with plausible but incorrect content.

Combined degradation: LaMa again ranks best. This makes LaMa the most consistent core method across all four approved degradation families.

6. Severity and affected area

Severity effects use within-painting Theil–Sen slopes. Affected-area associations use within-family painting-clustered Spearman analysis. Both preserve the five-painting independent-unit boundary.

Dirt Dust -0.861 -0.861 0.686

Water Stain 0.079 0.118 0.207
  • Water-stain slopes are slightly adverse for all three core methods.
  • Dirt/dust and partial-transparency slopes are not uniformly monotonic across models.
  • Larger water-stain areas tend to be more adverse descriptively, while several dirt/dust and partial-transparency associations are negative.
  • 0 model-severity rows and 0 affected-area rows remain significant after FDR correction.

What this means: the experiment does not support a universal rule that a higher configured severity or larger affected area always makes every model worse. Water stain shows the clearest adverse tendency, but the five-painting evidence remains limited.

7. Combined versus individual degradations

The moderate water-stain-and-dirt case is compared separately with its moderate water-stain and dirt/dust components. Positive values mean the combined computational case was harder.

model_id Compared single component OpenCV Telea LaMa Stable Diffusion
Water Stain -0.012 -0.184 0.015
Dirt Dust 0.706 0.255 0.135

Compared with dirt and dust alone: the combined case is harder for all three core models, with the largest median penalty for Telea. Telea therefore handles the ordered combined input worse than its dirt/dust component.

Compared with water stain alone: the pattern is mixed. LaMa has a negative median penalty, while Stable Diffusion is close to zero. The combined image is therefore not simply harder than both individual components.

This is an ordered RGB computation, not a physical degradation interaction experiment. It cannot establish moisture–dirt synergy, material chemistry, or treatment difficulty.

8. Evidence beyond pixel similarity

The comparison intentionally extends beyond pixel error. It retains perceptual, feature, spatial, texture, colour, seam, local semantic, and structural-layout evidence.

Evidence anchor Winner
Classical Masked Mae LaMa
Colour Masked Delta E LaMa
Feature Clip Crop Stable Diffusion
Feature Dino Crop Stable Diffusion
Perceptual Crop Lpips LaMa
Seam Boundary Gradient LaMa
Semantic Local Dino LaMa
Spatial Masked Error LaMa
Structural Affinity Correlation LaMa

What the anchors show: LaMa wins 8 of eleven anchors, Stable Diffusion wins 2, and Telea wins 1. LaMa is therefore better across the broadest set of evidence types, not only on one pixel metric.

Stable Diffusion's feature-similarity wins show why multiple metrics are necessary: semantic or feature affinity can remain strong even when visible local artifacts and reference-fidelity failures remain. Those wins do not overturn its weaker overall correction rank.

9. Failures and metric disagreement

Candidate failure profiles count improved, worsened, and tied anchors separately. They do not collapse those outcomes into a failure score.

Model Candidates Mean worsened anchors Median worsened anchors Mean improved anchors
LaMa 50 8.78 11.0 2.14
OpenCV Telea 50 8.96 11.0 1.98
SDXL 6 11.00 11.0 0.00
Stable Diffusion 50 10.78 11.0 0.16
  • Telea produces conspicuous radial smearing when a large contiguous region must be reconstructed.
  • LaMa generally preserves the best metric balance but can smooth texture and remove local detail.
  • Stable Diffusion can reconstruct semantically plausible objects while changing identity, structure, clothing, texture, or local composition.
  • Dirt and dust can remain visible or be replaced by newly generated speckle-like detail.

What this means: LaMa is better overall, but it is not failure-free. Stable Diffusion's semantic plausibility can conceal reference changes, while Telea's large-region failures are often visually obvious. Trustworthy review therefore requires both metrics and images.

These are computational and visual observations from selected cases. They are not independent human ratings, historical-authenticity judgements, or conservation decisions.

10. SDXL bounded subset

SDXL completed six predeclared synthetic-degradation cases at one seed. The same six cases have Telea, LaMa, and Stable Diffusion candidates, allowing a bounded four-model description.

Model Mean rank Median rank Best rank Worst rank
OpenCV Telea 2.442 2.600 1.50 3.1
LaMa 1.517 1.550 1.00 2.0
Stable Diffusion 2.525 2.375 2.20 3.0
SDXL 3.517 3.525 2.95 4.0

Subset conclusion: LaMa has the best mean rank inside the six-case subset. SDXL's displayed restorations can make large semantic changes, so the subset does not provide evidence that SDXL is a better restoration method.

Six cases, one seed, and imbalanced severity coverage cannot support a full SDXL comparison or a general four-model ranking.

Runtime is reported as operational evidence and is excluded from every quality rank, winner vote, and restoration conclusion.

OpenCV Telea 50 0.616 0.619 0.354 1.020

Operational conclusion: OpenCV Telea has the lowest median recorded candidate runtime. This makes it computationally faster in the recorded environment, but does not make it the better restoration method.

Runtime depends on hardware, implementation, batching, caching, software versions, and system load. LaMa and diffusion runtimes may also reflect different upstream accounting policies.

Each category contains one painting. A painting-specific difference cannot be separated from a category or style effect.

13. Supported conclusions and limits

Supported conclusions

  • LaMa is the strongest core correction method for the approved synthetic-degradation population.
  • Telea is competitive for sparse dirt/dust correction but becomes visibly weak over large contiguous affected areas.
  • Stable Diffusion retains useful feature and semantic affinity but is worse overall for reference-aligned degradation correction.
  • Model performance depends on degradation family, painting, and the evidence type used for evaluation.
  • Exact compositing prevents outside-mask pixel changes but does not guarantee a successful repair.
  • Metric disagreement is informative and must remain visible.

Unsupported conclusions

  • These procedural effects are not exact conservation damage.
  • The experiment does not establish physical degradation interaction.
  • It does not estimate independent category or style effects.
  • It does not establish historical authenticity or conservation approval.
  • The six-case SDXL subset does not establish full SDXL performance.
  • Runtime is not quality evidence.
  • Synthetic-degradation uncertainty is not applicable because no repeated-seed synthetic population exists in Notebooks 18 or 19.

Final scoped conclusion: LaMa is the better computational restoration choice for these eligible procedural corrections. That result supports model selection within the experiment, while human and conservation review remain necessary for real paintings.

14. Contribution to the thesis

RQ1 — How should restoration quality be evaluated?

The results show that no single metric is sufficient. Pixel, perceptual, feature, colour, texture, seam, semantic, structural, and visual evidence expose different strengths and failures.

Notebook 25 supports a multi-evidence evaluation framework and rejects a single combined quality or trust score.

RQ2 — How do restoration models compare?

LaMa provides the strongest overall correction balance. Telea remains useful for sparse localized effects, while diffusion methods can produce plausible but reference-changing content.

Model choice should depend on the restoration objective and failure risk, not only on visual plausibility.

RQ3 — What makes the evaluation trustworthy?

Trust comes from explicit eligibility, fixed candidate selection, region containment, metric disagreement, independent-unit inference, bounded claims, embedded visual evidence, and transparent unavailable evidence.

Repeated-seed uncertainty is not available for these synthetic cases. Recording that boundary is more trustworthy than inventing or borrowing uncertainty values.
